epigraph.quote: “Power Connect is the latest innovation supporting our speed-to-power advantage.” [23]
epigraph.author: Joe Tavi, Head of Bloom Energy’s Customer Installation Group

web_blocks.text: Bloom’s route to market combines direct selling with a financing and channel ecosystem. The FY2025 Form 10-K says the company sells Energy Servers to end users, financiers, strategic partners and international channel providers. In many customer arrangements the end user prefers to buy electricity rather than equipment; a financing partner purchases the server and supplies energy under a lease, capacity agreement or PPA. Bloom may then contract for maintenance directly with the end user. You should therefore distinguish the legal buyer, asset owner, electricity user and service customer when interpreting concentration, backlog and revenue. A named data-center customer is not automatically Bloom’s direct equipment customer. [1]

The sales and delivery path explains why this channel is useful and why results can be lumpy. Bloom’s Q3 2026 10-Q describes a typical sales cycle of 8–12 months, with large AI and data-center opportunities sometimes longer, and six to twelve months or more from sales contract to installation. Customer credit, financing, tax-equity appetite, gas availability, permits, construction, electrical interconnection, weather, customer access and acceptance can all delay delivery. Some steps are outside Bloom’s control. Thus the sales team’s initial customer win must pass through underwriting, construction and commissioning before the equipment appears as recognized revenue. [2]

Financing expands the addressable customer set by reducing the end user’s upfront capital outlay. It also means Bloom depends on third parties to assess project and customer credit, commit capital and monetize applicable tax benefits. The FY2025 filing describes a prospective Brookfield framework of up to $5 billion; the June 2026 release later said that framework had expanded to $25 billion. These figures describe a financing framework for qualifying future AI-infrastructure projects, not current cash on Bloom’s balance sheet or product revenue. You should evaluate the framework by projects actually financed, equipment transferred and contracts fulfilled. [1][22]

The service channel begins after delivery. Bloom describes first-year maintenance and optional annual extensions; its FY2025 filing says service contracts can run five to twenty years, subject to customer annual termination rights in relevant structures. Service revenue is generally recognized over the contract period. The company states that nearly every customer has historically renewed maintenance, which is favorable evidence of customer retention. Yet renewal may be economically attractive to the customer because a renewal price can be below the standalone service price; the company also carries performance obligations and possible guaranty payments. A high renewal rate is valuable only if the service cohort can be maintained profitably. [1]

For unit-economics work, set the boundary around delivered kilowatt-hours and reliability. Revenue may include equipment, installation, service and retained electricity. Costs include raw materials and supplier components, factory labor and overhead, shipping, installation labor, fuel where Bloom retains the obligation, service visits, module replacement, warranties and performance guarantees. The customer’s own comparison depends on local gas prices, grid tariffs, operating profile, incentive qualification and avoided downtime. DOE’s technology overview notes the system-level fuel processor and power conditioner; the cell’s conversion efficiency is not the same as the customer’s delivered cost. No site-level lifetime cost or realized savings is inferred here from marketing claims. [1][10][12][24]

web_blocks.text: This category table highlights the difference between factory economics and project economics. Product gross margin was 37.9%, service margin 17.8%, electricity margin 25.7%, while installation margin was negative 4.8% in Q3 2026. The company’s total gross margin was 33.8%. Installation outcomes can vary with project mix and timing; in Q3 2025 the reported installation margin had been positive. The correct inference is not that installation must always lose money, but that installation can absorb value even when product sales are profitable. A business-level assessment should follow all four categories and contractual obligations together. [3]

Bloom’s supply chain is concentrated around manufacturing in the United States and a network of suppliers for specialized materials and subassemblies. Its filings identify rare-earth components, tariffs, supplier quality, labor and availability as potential constraints. A factory expansion can reduce unit cost through scale but can also create fixed investment and inventory before customer acceptance. Bloom’s 2025 filing described capacity expansion plans toward approximately 2 GW at Fremont by the end of 2026; the 2026 filing reports significant capital spending and continuing production investment. You should treat capacity as an input measure until the site reaches output, quality and utilization targets. [1][2]

Power Connect targets one operational bottleneck: onsite electrical integration. Bloom says the new approach shifts substantial wiring and testing from the customer site into factory-prepared assemblies and claims an installation-time reduction exceeding 40%. Joe Tavi said, “It reflects how we’re rethinking the entire power deployment process, moving complexity out of the field and into a controlled manufacturing process.” [23] That is a testable process claim. The diligence question is whether it reduces site hours, variance, rework and acceptance delays without increasing factory cost or limiting customization. Until Bloom reports completed cohorts, use the announcement as a proposed process improvement, not a proven margin benefit. [23]

The customer-level margin stack also depends on fuel and regulatory conditions. Bloom’s systems require a continuous fuel supply, while a facility’s available gas volume, gas pressure, fuel specification and local permitting can differ. DOE identifies fuel flexibility as a characteristic of solid oxide systems but also notes high-temperature durability and start-up limitations. California’s fuel-cell-specific net-metering tariff closed to new customers at the end of 2023, according to Bloom’s filing; permits and tariffs can alter the economics of exports. Islanded systems may avoid some grid-interconnection requirements but still need site, gas, fire, air and construction approvals. [1][2][10]

The distribution model’s central trade-off is clear. Financiers and channel partners can bring more customers into the funnel and hold project assets, while Bloom can focus on equipment and long-term service. But the partner layer can lengthen diligence, concentrate direct revenue in a few counterparties and expose projects to financing markets. The 2025 top-three customer revenue shares were 43%, 13% and 12%. To judge whether distribution improves business quality, track counterparty concentration alongside end-user diversity, customer credit, financed capacity, delivery timing and service renewal—not just the count of announced megawatts. [1]

Bloom’s route from order to cash has multiple checkpoints. The order must be executable under contract; the customer or financier must close funding; required permits and infrastructure must be ready; equipment must be manufactured to specification; field work must be completed; and the customer must accept the installation. Then service begins, with future maintenance expense and performance commitments. Each stage determines whether the initial gross-profit opportunity becomes a durable relationship or a write-down, delay or guarantee expense. The later chapters preserve that operational chain as the unit of analysis. [1][2][3]

Backlog also needs careful interpretation. Bloom defines product backlog as revenue attributable to existing contractual commitments for future purchase or use of Energy Servers and says its value can reflect anticipated investment tax credits and other incentives. Service backlog includes contracted O&M revenue associated with installed and committed systems. The filing warns that timing of delivery, permitting, customer construction and financing can delay recognition, and that annual service renewals may be terminable. A backlog figure, when reviewed later, should therefore be decomposed by product versus service, financing status, site readiness, customer acceptance and incentive assumptions. [1]

The supplier problem is not simply whether a component can be purchased. Bloom says supplier quality failures or late delivery can affect manufacturing, servicing, customer schedules and warranty obligations. Specialized materials may be difficult to replace on short notice. Growing output can increase supplier concentration or expose the company to tariffs, while design changes intended to reduce material needs may require qualification and field testing. You should ask whether manufacturing growth is supported by qualified alternatives, inventory policy and quality controls rather than extrapolating from a stated nameplate capacity. [1]

Contract terms can also shift economic risk between Bloom, the financier and the end user. Bloom describes product warranties, efficiency and output guarantees, and performance reimbursements that are generally capped by contract. A system sold before it is installed may carry a warranty period tied to commencement of operations; an extended maintenance service is a separate obligation in some arrangements. You should read those clauses alongside the revenue category and margin: the seller may recognize product revenue while retaining obligations whose cost appears later through warranty accrual, service expense or reductions to revenue. [1][2]

book_paragraphs: As your mentor, I want you to map the route to market before looking at any growth headline. First identify who signs the equipment purchase. Then identify who owns the Energy Server, who consumes the electricity and who buys ongoing service. Bloom says those parties can differ. A financier or strategic partner may buy the system while an enterprise customer buys power and Bloom supplies maintenance. That structure can make onsite generation more accessible to an end user, but it also creates counterparty, financing and concentration risk. When the filings say “customer,” do not automatically substitute the building where the electrons are consumed. [1]

Now follow the project clock. Bloom’s Q3 2026 filing places a typical sales cycle at 8–12 months and says large AI/data-center opportunities may run longer; contract to installation generally takes six to twelve months or more. During that interval you should expect financing, permitting, gas and electric interconnection, construction, delivery, installation and acceptance to interact. A system may be technically ready while the customer’s facility is not. That is why a signed contract can still fail to produce the period’s expected revenue. You are assessing project execution as well as product demand. [2]

Financing is not a footnote to the distribution strategy. It is often the mechanism by which a customer avoids owning a large equipment asset. A financing partner evaluates customer credit and project economics; interest rates, tax incentives and capital availability can change the decision. Brookfield’s expanded $25-billion framework is described as a structure to finance qualifying future projects, not a cash balance or an automatic guarantee. You should trace each financing announcement to named projects, closing, installation and revenue recognition. [1][22]

Service creates a second relationship after commissioning. Bloom reports five-to-twenty-year O&M terms in some agreements, but the customer may have annual renewal or cancellation rights. The company says nearly every customer historically renewed maintenance, which supports retention. The economic caveat is that a customer’s renewal price may be attractive relative to a standalone service contract, while the vendor remains responsible for maintenance and performance commitments. You should measure renewal alongside repair frequency, module replacement, field labor and guarantee payments. An installed base is an asset only if it remains supportable. [1]

Build a simple customer-level economics model in words before attempting a number. Start with usable output and required availability. Then account for fuel, equipment, installation, financing, service, replacements, insurance and local tariffs. Compare that package with the actual grid alternative and customer’s downtime cost. Do not assume that a cell-level efficiency figure equals a lower bill, and do not assume that the company’s disclosed gross margin equals the customer’s project return. DOE’s component overview helps you see why the system boundary includes fuel processing and power conditioning. [10][12][24]

Q3 2026 category margins show you why those distinctions matter. Product gross margin was 37.9%, service was 17.8%, electricity was 25.7%, and installation was negative 4.8%, producing a total company margin of 33.8%. These are period results, not lifetime margins. Installation may be profitable or unprofitable according to scope, project size and completion timing. If you focused only on the product margin, you would overlook project costs; if you focused only on one quarter’s installation loss, you would overlook the factory contribution. [3]

A supplier base and factory are also part of unit economics. Bloom’s filings identify specialized components, rare-earth materials, supplier quality, tariffs and workforce needs. Expansion toward approximately 2 GW at Fremont is a company plan; the Q3 2026 10-Q records sizable plant spending. You should test actual output, yields, lead times and utilization against the capacity plan. More capacity can create purchasing leverage, but it also increases working capital and the cost of unused factory assets if order conversion slows. [1][2]

Power Connect provides a concrete example of the company trying to change project economics through design. Bloom says assemblies will arrive pre-connected, pre-wired and tested, with a claimed installation-time reduction exceeding 40%. Joe Tavi said the approach moves complexity from the field into factory-controlled work. You should make that claim measurable: field electrician hours, commissioning variance, rework, time from delivery to acceptance and installation gross margin. Until disclosed evidence covers multiple deployments, the system is a promising operational hypothesis, not a demonstrated margin improvement. [23]

Fuel economics and regulation are site-specific. Natural gas supply may be available in one region and constrained in another; local gas and electricity prices affect customer comparisons. Tariff rules determine whether unused output can be exported and compensated. Bloom disclosed the end of California’s special fuel-cell net-metering tariff for new customers and ongoing emissions and permitting requirements. Islanded operation can reduce exposure to a grid queue but does not eliminate air, gas, fire, zoning or safety review. You should not confuse a shorter interconnection path with a permit-free installation. [1][2][10]

Your distribution scorecard should therefore put customer concentration next to repeat orders. Bloom’s top three revenue customers were about 43%, 13% and 12% of sales in FY2025. Channel and financing relationships can make the business scale, but the same channel can concentrate recognized revenue. Ask whether end users diversify even when invoice customers do not, whether project financing remains available, whether installations are accepted on time and whether service economics are retained by Bloom. [1]

Finally, follow each project all the way to cash. An order is only the start. Funding, permits, materials, assembly, delivery, installation and acceptance must occur; then the system must perform well enough to sustain renewals without excessive guarantees. This sequence explains both the growth opportunity and the execution risk. The same operational discipline that creates an efficient distribution model can turn field learning into a moat; weak coordination can turn a seemingly strong backlog into a delay and a margin shortfall. [1][2][3]

You should treat backlog as a claim on future conversion, not as cash already earned. Bloom’s FY2025 filing defines product backlog as future revenue attributable to contractual commitments and says its value may reflect anticipated incentives. Service backlog is separate and may be associated with systems already operating or still to be delivered. The company also describes delays from permits, construction and financing, and service extensions can be terminable annually. When you revisit backlog, ask what share is financed, site-ready, installed, accepted and collectible. [1]

The pricing and margin stack matters at customer level even when you remain price-blind about the equity. A customer’s energy decision depends on local gas, utility tariffs, demand shape and downtime. Bloom’s own filing says the value of its Energy Server can change as those inputs change. You should avoid writing a universal savings claim because a favorable installation in one state or tariff environment may not reproduce elsewhere. The appropriate unit-economics question is whether the customer has a reason to pay for the actual reliability and deployment profile at that site, after financing, fuel and service are included. [1][24]

A high-temperature stack must be supported for years, and the service contract carries that obligation. Bloom’s filing describes first-year monitoring and performance commitments, plus optional extensions. If output or efficiency misses contractual levels, Bloom may repair or replace equipment or make capped payments. You should connect product design, spare parts, field-service staffing and warranty reserves. A strong product gross margin at shipment cannot tell you the final customer-cohort margin if the fleet later experiences higher service visits or performance-guarantee costs. [1][2][3]

The supplier network is another reason that a factory plan does not automatically become output. You need the component specification, qualified source, delivery lead time, defect rate and substitution plan. Bloom specifically discloses rare-earth and subassembly risks, tariffs and supplier quality concerns. A growing plant can improve purchasing leverage when the line is utilized, but early inventory accumulation and fixed-cost absorption may weaken cash flow if installations lag. The 2026 cash-flow statement’s inventory growth and the company’s disclosed expansion investment make this more than a theoretical issue. [1][2]

Now assess the Power Connect quotation with a skeptical but fair eye. Joe Tavi said the approach moves complexity from the field into a controlled manufacturing process. You should make that claim measurable: field electrician hours, commissioning variance, rework, time from delivery to acceptance and installation gross margin. Until disclosed evidence covers multiple deployments, the system is a promising operational hypothesis, not a demonstrated margin improvement. [23]

Your distribution scorecard should follow each project all the way to cash. An order is only the start. Funding, permits, materials, assembly, delivery, installation and acceptance must occur; then the system must perform well enough to sustain renewals without excessive guarantees. This sequence explains both the growth opportunity and the execution risk. The same operational discipline that creates an efficient distribution model can turn field learning into a moat; weak coordination can turn a seemingly strong backlog into a delay and a margin shortfall. [1][2][3]

You should read a financing contract as a distribution choice and a risk allocation at once. A PPA can help a customer use onsite power without purchasing the server, yet someone must own the equipment, raise capital, bear fuel and operating obligations and collect payments. Bloom’s filings explain that contract terms may separate the equipment buyer from the service customer and may include capped performance guarantees. That structure can accelerate a sale, but it also creates counterparties and obligations that affect recognized revenue and lifetime margin. [1]

You can read the FY2025 waterfall as two linked statements, not as a fabricated payroll bridge. The audited P&L reports $2,023.994 million revenue, $1,436.594 million cost of revenue, $514.598 million operating expenses and $72.802 million operating income. The cash-flow statement reports $50.566 million D&A, $113.949 million CFO and $56.759 million PP&E purchases. Interest expense was $53.888 million, but interest income and other non-operating items are separately disclosed. Bloom does not publish a standalone employee-cost total, so you should leave that allocation unavailable rather than treat it as zero. [1]

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: You have just seen why the unit of analysis is not one product margin. The customer buys a system through a contract, a financing path and an installation process, then judges the vendor over years of service. Your checklist should follow the counterparty, cash source, permit, supplier, commissioning result and renewal. If any one of those steps is missing, the promise of a repeatable onsite-power sale is not yet a repeatable business.
